newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU says Boeing must make concessions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU says Boeing must make concessions.

text.p: U.S. aircraft manufacturer Boeing must make concessions to win European Union regulatory approval for its merger with McDonnell Douglas, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Tuesday.

Reiterating that the Commission had strong concerns about the impact of the $14 billion merger on competition, Van Miert said he was determined to pursue the investigation to the end and would not give in to political pressure.

"We try to go as far as possible regarding cooperation (with the United States), but it is clear that we must obtain remedies that meet our concerns," he told the European Parliament economic and monetary affairs committee.
"We are determined to pursue the proceedings until the end," he added.
Van Miert again denied suggestions that the Commission does not have the power to impose any conditions on the deal because both companies are located outside the EU.
He noted that the United States itself had long claimed jurisdiction over non-U.S. deals, citing a merger between Swiss drug companies Sandoz and Ciba Geigy.
"If the Commission must take a negative decision, if Boeing does not offer remedies, this merger will be illegal in one of the world's largest markets," Van Miert said.
While some deputies expressed scepticism about how much power the Commission had to impose its will, Van Miert said his options included slapping fines on the companies.
"We still have a few instruments and there should not be any doubt as to our determination to use those instruments if necessary," he said.

Under EU law, the Commission must probe all mergers or acquisitions involving companies with a worldwide turnover of five billion European currency units ($5.6 billion) and EU sales of 250 million Ecus ($280 million) each, irrespective of their nationality.

The 1990 merger law allows the Commission to seek concessions, usually in the form of asset sell-offs, in return for its clearance. But if the companies fail to provide remedies that ensure fair competition, it may block the deal altogether.
Van Miert has made it clear that the Boeing merger will not go through as it stands.
He particularly took aim at recent long-term exclusive supply contracts signed with AMR's American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and Continental Airlines as reflecting Boeing's strong position.

The Commission is under increasing pressure to set tough conditions on the merger after Europe's Airbus Industrie , the companies' only big rival, said bluntly last weekend that it could not survive if the deal went through. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
